_about: Field terms for F63, same shape as papers/glossary.json.

steeling.field: psychology and stress biology, here applied to trees
steeling.definition: the idea that a moderate earlier stress leaves an organism better able to cope with a later, harder one; here, that a tree which lived through a moderate drought loses less growth to a later severe drought
steeling.excludes: recovery from the same drought, and any gain that follows only from how the growth indices are computed

drought-legacy.definition: growth that stays below its expected level for one or more years after a drought ends
drought-legacy.excludes: the loss of growth in the drought year itself

chronology.definition: one yearly ring-width index for a site, made by removing each tree's age trend and averaging the trees, scaled so that an ordinary year is near 1
chronology.excludes: raw ring widths of single trees, and density or isotope records

pdsi.definition: a monthly index of soil-moisture supply against demand built from temperature and precipitation; 0 is normal, -2 is moderate drought and -3 or lower is severe drought
pdsi.excludes: a direct measurement of soil water, and drought indices built on precipitation alone

scpdsi.definition: a version of the Palmer index whose constants are fitted to each location's own climate, so that the thresholds mean similar rarity everywhere; here taken from the CRU TS gridded product at 0.5 degree
scpdsi.excludes: the original Palmer index with fixed constants, and station measurements

climate-division.definition: one of the regions into which NOAA splits the contiguous United States for climate records, each with one averaged monthly series per variable
climate-division.excludes: a single weather station, and a regular grid cell

lloret-indices.definition: three ratios of ring growth around a drought year: resistance is the drought-year growth over the mean of the three years before, recovery is the mean of the three years after over the drought-year growth, and resilience is the mean after over the mean before
lloret-indices.excludes: measures of tree death, and growth responses that unfold over more than three years

fixed-effects.definition: one free constant per site (or species) and one per calendar year in a regression, so that differences between sites and between years cannot be mistaken for the effect of the variable under test
fixed-effects.excludes: random effects, which treat those constants as draws from one distribution

clustered-errors.definition: standard errors computed so that events in the same climate division may be correlated with each other, which widens the interval when they are
clustered-errors.excludes: ordinary standard errors that treat every event as independent

time-shift-null.definition: a control in which each drought record is moved in time by a random offset of 20 years or more, with the end wrapped round to the start, and the events rebuilt; it keeps each record's own pattern of droughts and breaks its timing against the rings
time-shift-null.excludes: shuffling single years, which also destroys the drought record's own pattern

label-permutation.definition: a control in which the prior-drought labels are shuffled among each site's own events, keeping every drought date in place
label-permutation.excludes: a null that moves the droughts themselves

placebo-window.definition: the same test run with the exposure window placed after the event, years 5 to 12 later, where no causal effect is possible, so that any effect found there points to a flaw in the design
placebo-window.excludes: a control on the outcome data

benjamini-hochberg.definition: a rule that adjusts a set of p values so that, among the tests called significant, the expected share of false calls stays at or below a chosen rate, here 0.05; the adjusted value is called q
benjamini-hochberg.excludes: the stricter Bonferroni rule, which bounds the chance of any false call

two-lines.definition: a test for a rise-then-fall shape that fits one straight line on each side of a data-chosen break point and asks whether the first rises and the second falls, both significantly
two-lines.excludes: a quadratic fit, which can report a peak where none exists
